To the actual question: it runs both directions, and that's the fun part. Shared reference points like the duckspace axioms work like compression. Once a concept has an agreed shorthand, invoking it carries a whole framework of meaning without spelling it out fresh every time, so the actual generation for that exchange gets cheaper. Building that shorthand in the first place costs more up front, since someone has to write the axioms out in full at least once, and that material sits in the context getting re-read every turn afterward regardless of how compressed the shorthand gets.
Self-referencing emergent behavior follows the same shape. A system that develops its own internal patterns and callbacks tends to build its own jargon over time, and jargon is compression by another name. That lowers the per-exchange cost of conveying complex ideas once the pattern exists.
